title: The Guru bows to the disciple
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas marvels that Nanak bowed to Angad, making the disciple the Guru (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

lines: BABA NANAK CHOOSES WHO COMES NEXT.
A HANDOVER THE OTHER WAY ROUND.
cards: A handover at work tends to go one way. The old boss signs the papers, gives a short speech, maybe cuts a cake, and walks out the door, and the new one is still, somehow, the junior.

Near the end of his first var, Bhai Gurdas tells a handover that runs the other way round. Baba Nanak chooses the one who will carry the light after him, and then does something that makes Bhai Gurdas marvel.

teach.b: Bhai Gurdas says that while Nanak was still living, he set Lehna in the Guru's place and had the canopy held over his head, the sign of the Guru's seat. He gave him a new name, Angad.
And Bhai Gurdas treats it as a wonder: the master bowing to the one he'd chosen.
The bow is sung in the Guru Granth Sahib too, in the var of Satta and Balwand on Ang nine hundred sixty-six: the Guru bowed to the disciple while Nanak was still alive.
Bhai Gurdas pictures it as light merging into light. Nanak's light didn't go out. It wasn't handed along like a lamp passed from one hand to another, leaving the first hand empty.
It merged: the same light, now in a new form.

Sikhs often sum it up in a phrase that turns the order upside down: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru. In Sikh teaching, Guruship isn't a possession to clutch until the end.
It's a light, and the one who carries it is the first to bow to it when it shines in someone else.
Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit, and the pattern carries into Sikh life now, where Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

Bowing to someone you taught means trusting that what you gave them is theirs now, and might grow in their hands in ways it never could in yours. Nanak, in Bhai Gurdas's telling, does it with the Guru's own seat.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's handing on to Guru Angad, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as one light passing into a new form, and today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

games.q: you're Baba Nanak. you've chosen the one who'll carry the light after you. what do you do?
o: keep the seat to the very end, then let it pass.
set him in the Guru's place while you live, and bow to him.
leave the choice to the crowd.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak, while living, set Lehna in the Guru's seat, named him Angad and bowed to him: the Guru became the disciple.

practice: Bring to mind someone younger who knows something you don't: a niece who knows the app, a new colleague who sees an old problem fresh, a teenager who once corrected you and turned out to be right.
Picture asking them, simply, show me, and notice whatever in you resists that, and let it soften a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Angad, the name Nanak gave Lehna when he placed him in the Guru's seat and bowed to him: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: light, a flame. Bhai Gurdas pictures the handover as light merging into light.

carryVoice: Your line: the teacher bows. The light stayed whole as it moved. See you tomorrow.
